title: India now gets more oil from the Gulf than from Russia
subtitle: Tankers are moving through the Strait of Hormuz again, and Indian refiners are going back to their old Gulf suppliers.
content_html:
Here is a big shift in where India gets its oil. On Thursday, 12 November 2026, Business Standard carried a Bloomberg report with fresh numbers. For the first time since the Iran war began, India is getting more crude oil from the Persian Gulf than from Russia. So far in November, 2.1 million barrels a day have reached India through the Strait of Hormuz, against 1.8 million barrels a day from Russia, according to the energy data firm Kpler.

Just a few months ago the picture looked very different. In April, the flow of oil through Hormuz to India had dropped to only 247,000 barrels a day. In February, before the trouble, the average was 2.8 million barrels a day. Attacks on ships had more or less closed the waterway. Now the tap is running again.

Where does India's oil come from?

Crude oil is the thick black liquid that comes out of the ground. Refineries turn it into petrol, diesel, cooking gas and jet fuel. India does not dig up nearly enough of it at home. In April to September 2026, 88.1 per cent of the crude oil India used came from abroad, says government data from the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC), reported by ThePrint.

Bloomberg calls India the world's third largest oil buyer. For years its main sellers were the Gulf countries: Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Iraq and Kuwait. Then Russia joined the list in a big way, and became India's biggest single supplier.

Think of a family that buys rice from two shops. One shop is close by and has been their shop for years. The other is far away but gives a big discount. When the road to the near shop is blocked, the far shop gets all the business. When the road opens again, the family goes back to the near shop, if the price is right.

What is a chokepoint?

A chokepoint is a narrow gate on a very busy road. Picture a stadium with 50,000 fans and just one exit gate. If that gate gets stuck, nobody can leave, however wide the stadium is.

The Strait of Hormuz is that kind of narrow sea gate. Gulf oil bound for India sails out through it. When ships were attacked there this year, tankers stopped coming, and India had to look elsewhere for oil. The war between the US and Iran caused the trouble; here the focus is only the oil.

Why did Russia matter so much?

After Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, buyers in Europe stopped buying Russian oil. To find new buyers, Moscow offered steep discounts, and India became a major customer. News agency PTI reported that Russian oil grew from almost nothing to as much as 40 to 50 per cent of India's crude basket at the peak.

The discount was huge. In late 2022 and early 2023, Russian Urals crude at times traded about $30 a barrel below Brent, says the same PTI report. Brent is a global benchmark price for crude oil, a bit like the MRP printed on a packet. Getting oil $30 below Brent was like a samosa stall buying potatoes far below the market rate.

That discount has now almost vanished, PTI reports. But when Gulf oil could not get through Hormuz this year, Russian oil filled the gap, as Bloomberg notes.

So why the switch now?

Three things changed, as the Bloomberg report describes.

  • Tankers found a way through. Ships now make short back and forth trips through Hormuz. The oil then moves onto the buyers' own tankers outside the waterway. It is like a relay race, where one runner hands the baton to the next.
  • Gulf sellers are offering good prices. Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Iraq and Kuwait together shipped 15.53 million barrels a day in October, roughly the level of the start of the year.
  • Russian oil now costs more to bring home. Freight, the charge for carrying goods by ship, has gone up, and Russian voyages are longer. Freight works like the delivery fee on a food app: a cheap biryani with a big delivery fee is not cheap anymore.

Russia also has its own trouble. Ukrainian attacks on its energy sites have hurt Russian oil sales abroad. Its oil shipments to other countries fell by 40,000 barrels a day to 3.63 million in the four weeks to 8 November, according to tanker data compiled by Bloomberg.

This shift did not come out of nowhere. India's crude imports reached a record of about 5.6 million barrels a day in October, PTI reported, citing Kpler. Of that, about 2.3 million barrels a day came from the Middle East and around 2 million from Russia. In September, ThePrint reported, using Kpler data, Russian supply to India dropped to about 1.74 million barrels a day, the lowest since April.

Kpler's lead analyst Nikhil Dubey had warned that Russian flows "could soften in November-December as attacks in the Black Sea push freight rates higher, making Russian barrels less attractive on a landed cost basis." The landed cost is the full price of oil once it reaches an Indian port, including the ship ride.

What this means for fuel prices and India's bill

Oil is one of the biggest things India buys from the world. In April to September 2026, India's crude oil import bill jumped 46.3 per cent to $90.6 billion, up from $61.9 billion a year earlier, according to the PPAC data reported by ThePrint.

Here is the surprising part. India bought almost the same amount of oil: 122.7 million tonnes, against 121.8 million tonnes a year before. The bill grew because each barrel cost more. The Indian basket, the average price India pays, was $116.09 a barrel in September 2026, against $69.61 in September 2025.

Why should a student care? Think of a canteen that pays more for milk. Sooner or later, the cup of chai may cost more. In the same way, ThePrint notes that a long spell of high crude prices could push up inflation, mainly through fuel and transport costs. Inflation means prices of everyday things going up, so your pocket money buys less.

Having more sellers helps. When India can pick between Gulf oil and Russian oil, refiners can go for the better deal. PTI reported that Gulf suppliers are offering keen prices, delivered to India, to win back their share of India's purchases.

Can the picture change again?

Yes, and quickly. Dubey said, as PTI reported, that any new trouble in Hormuz could see Indian refiners turning back to Russian oil, even at higher freight costs. Russia is not going away either. "Russia remains a central part of India's crude import basket," Kpler's Sumit Ritolia told ThePrint.

So India now has two big taps. It can turn one up when the other runs slow. For a country that buys most of its oil abroad, that choice is worth a lot.
